findings.text: The opening says plainly what Athena is and what makes it different, so a newcomer learns that much in the first few lines.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: This is Athena's home URL, but after the three intro paragraphs nearly the whole page is about another project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets about two sentences on it, and then a long, detailed study of a tool they may never have heard of.
findings.source: Title: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"; sections "States of a piece of work", "Transitions", "Claims and sources"

findings.text: The page does say why it exists: it shows off Athena's ability to cite its sources. But it never links that ability back to Athena's main job of turning a request into a code change, so the reader can't easily tell how the study shows what Athena does for them.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: There is a link to the next steps right in the header, so the reader can skip the study. That helps.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

findings.text: The install steps are too thin to follow. They skip cloning the repository, say nothing about prerequisites (Rust? API keys for the two AI models?), and don't say what `athena ask` will do or produce.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" / "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: For a reader who does want the firstmate study, the "Start here" section is well built. It covers terms first, then a one-paragraph summary, then a numbered walk through one task, then failure cases.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails or has no limit."

findings.text: Even the introductory part goes into exit codes, lock contention and transition ids that haven't been explained yet. A newcomer will find this dense.
findings.source: "If every place of a declared capacity is held, the spawn exits 75 and the item stays queued." and Counters: "changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: Admitting what the source doesn't say is honest. It's useful to a careful reader, though it may confuse a newcomer who expects a definition.
findings.source: in scope: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: This section refers to an internal folder of a repository the reader hasn't seen, so it means nothing to a newcomer.
findings.source: About this page: "This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
